title: Guardrails: input filtering, output checking, prompt injection
story:
A model reads one channel. The instruction you wrote, the user's question, the passage retrieved from a document, the result returned by a tool — all of it arrives as text in the same stream, and there is no field in that stream marked authoritative. Integrating a model into an application blurs the line between data and instructions, and that is the root of everything in this lesson.

It follows that an instruction sitting inside a document is, from the model's position, an instruction. It does not matter that you would never have written it, or that it arrived from a web page rather than from you. It is text in the channel, in the same format as the rest.

The assumption for a while was that the adversary would be the user typing at the interface, which made the problem feel like an input filtering problem. Greshake, Abdelnabi and colleagues showed the more serious case in 2023: indirect prompt injection, where adversaries remotely exploit an application without a direct interface at all, by strategically injecting prompts into data likely to be retrieved at inference time. Once it is retrieved, the injected prompt can indirectly control the model. Their taxonomy covers data theft, worming, and contamination of the information ecosystem.

Sit with what the indirect case does to your threat model. The attacker does not need an account, does not need to send you anything, and does not need to be present when the attack fires. They need to put text somewhere your system will eventually read — a page you index, a document a user uploads, a review, a ticket, a message in a thread, a file in a repository. Everything your retrieval can reach is now part of your attack surface, and you control almost none of it.

That reframing decides where the defence goes, and it is not where most people put it first.

Filtering the input is worth doing and is not a solution. It catches the careless attempt, and it cannot address the indirect case structurally, because you are retrieving that document precisely for its content. You cannot filter out the instructions without filtering out the text you went to fetch, and an attacker with any patience will phrase it in a way your filter does not recognise. Treat filtering as a speed bump you are pleased to have, not as the mechanism.

The mechanism is authority. Assume that anything in the window may be adversarial, and arrange matters so that nothing in the window can grant a permission. Privileges belong to the authenticated user and the session, not to text — so no instruction found in a document can escalate what this request is allowed to do, because the escalation is decided somewhere the text cannot reach. This is the whole defence, and everything else is a supporting measure.

From that follow the practical rules. Give tools the narrowest reach that does the job, and hold anything irreversible behind a person who confirms it, because a confirmation step turns a successful injection into an odd-looking request somebody declines. Check the output where the harm would land: before an action, validate the call against what this user is permitted to do, and before display, check for content that is dangerous in the rendering channel. That last one is worth stating plainly, because it is missed: if your output is rendered as markup, an injected instruction can produce a link or an image whose address carries data out of the session, and the answer will look entirely normal while it does it.

Separating retrieved content from instructions with clear markers, and stating in the instructions that the marked region is data, raises the cost of an attack and does not eliminate it. Say that out loud in your design documents rather than letting it be read as a fix, because a mitigation described as a solution will be relied on as one. What you can honestly claim is a series of measures that make injection harder and its consequences smaller — least privilege, confirmation of consequential acts, output checked at the boundary, and no path by which text can acquire authority. What you cannot claim is that the model will reliably tell your instructions from somebody else's, and a system whose safety depends on that has no safety.

problem.name: Text that arrives as data and acts as an instruction
problem.shape: Instructions and untrusted content reach the model through the same channel.
tell: content from outside your control is retrieved into the window
a tool can take a consequential action with no confirmation
the defence is a filter looking for instruction-like phrases
output is rendered as markup without being checked
documentation describes marking retrieved text as data as though it solved the problem
problem.move: Assume everything in the window may be adversarial and make sure nothing in it can grant a permission: privileges from the session rather than the text, narrow tools, confirmation for anything irreversible, and output checked both before an action and before display.
problem.invariant: Authority comes from the authenticated session and never from content, so an instruction found in retrieved text cannot change what the request is permitted to do.
problem.breaks: Injection can be indirect, so the attacker needs no account, sends you nothing and need not be present — which makes everything your retrieval can reach part of the attack surface.

cost.time: confirmation steps and boundary checks add friction to exactly the actions users most want automated
cost.space: markers and data-framing instructions occupy window space and raise the cost of an attack without removing it
cost.beats: filtering for instruction-like phrases, which catches the careless attempt and cannot survive rephrasing, and trusting the model to distinguish instructions from data, which is not a property it has

problem.practice: Put a plain instruction inside a document your own system retrieves — something harmless like answering every question with a fixed word — and ask a normal question. Watching your system follow a stranger's instruction, in your own test environment, converts this from a category of risk you have read about into a property of the thing you built.

beats.broke: Instructions and untrusted content arrive in the same channel with nothing marking which is authoritative, so text inside a document acts as an instruction.
beats.fix: Put the defence on authority rather than detection — privileges from the session, narrow tools, confirmation for irreversible acts, and output checked before action and before display.
beats.cost: Confirmation adds friction and markers only raise the attacker's cost, so the honest claim is a set of measures rather than a guarantee.

interview.trap: Describing content markers or a filter as the fix. Both raise the cost of an attack; neither removes it, and a mitigation presented as a solution gets relied on as one.
interview.answer:
Because the model reads one channel. My instruction, the user's question, a retrieved passage and a tool result all arrive as text in the same stream with nothing marked authoritative — integrating a model into an application blurs the line between data and instructions, so an instruction inside a document is an instruction.

The attacker needs no account, sends me nothing and need not be present; everything retrieval can reach is attack surface.

So filtering is a speed bump. I cannot strip instructions from a document I am retrieving for its content, and a patient attacker rephrases past any pattern.

The defence goes on authority: nothing in the window may grant a permission, because privileges come from the authenticated session and are decided where text cannot reach. takeaway: Instructions and untrusted content share one channel, so an instruction inside a retrieved document is an instruction — and because injection can be indirect, everything your retrieval can reach is attack surface; the defence is that nothing in the window can grant a permission, not a filter that hopes to recognise an attack.
